text: The Pakistan men's national field hockey team (Urdu: پاکستان قومى ہاكى ٹیم) represents Pakistan in international field hockey and has played its first match in 1948. It is administered by the Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF), which was established in 1948 following the country's independence, and has been a member of the International Hockey Federation (FIH) since 1948. Pakistan was also a founding member of the Asian Hockey Federation (ASHF), formed in 1958. The team is one of the most successful in the world, having won four Hockey World Cup titles in 1971, 1978, 1982, and 1994. Pakistan has participated in all FIH World Cup editions except 2014 and 2023. The Green Shirts are the most successful national team in the Asian Games with eight gold medals in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1974, 1978, 1982, 1990, and 2010, and the only Asian team to have won the Champions Trophy three times in 1978, 1980, and 1994. The team has secured a total of 29 official international titles, including three Olympic gold medals in Rome 1960, Mexico City 1968, and Los Angeles 1984. Field hockey is the national sport of Pakistan. The team was ranked world number one by the FIH in both 2000 and 2001. Former captain Sohail Abbas is the second-highest goalscorer in international field hockey history, while Waseem Ahmad is the most-capped player, having played 410 times between 1996 and 2013. Pakistan has a fierce rivalry with India, having played each other in 20 major tournament finals, winning 13 titles, and consecutively winning the first three Hockey Asia Cup championships in 1982, 1985, and 1989. Notable rivalries also exist with the Netherlands and Australia. The team's home ground is the National Hockey Stadium in Lahore, with current head coach Shahnaz Sheikh and team manager Saeed Khan. The game was introduced to British India by British servicemen and became popular, with players from pre-partition India representing Pakistan. After independence, the PHF established provincial associations in West Punjab, East Bengal, Sindh, Balochistan, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, Bahawalpur, and Services. Pakistan's first international match was on 8 August 1948 against Belgium, winning 2–1 at the 1948 London Olympics, where they remained unbeaten, defeating the Netherlands, Denmark, and France in the group stage, with a 6–1 win over the Netherlands being a highlight. They went on an undefeated tour of Europe, playing Belgium, Netherlands, and Italy. In 1950, Pakistan won its first international tournament by being declared joint winners with the Netherlands after a draw in a Spain invitational competition. In 1952, at the Helsinki Olympics, Pakistan won 6–0 against France in the first knockout game but lost to the Netherlands and Great Britain, finishing fourth. Between 1950 and 1956, Pakistan toured Europe and Asia, playing regularly in Malaysia and Singapore. At the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, Pakistan reached the final and lost 1–0 to India, earning its first Olympic medal—a silver. Field hockey was first included in the Asian Games in 1958 in Tokyo, where Pakistan beat Japan 5–0, South Korea 8–0, and Malaysia 6–0, drawing 0–0 with India to win its first gold. In 1960 Rome, Pakistan won all group matches against Australia, Poland, and Japan, defeated Germany 2–1 in the quarter-finals, beat Spain in the semi-finals, and won the gold medal by defeating India 1–0 in the final, with Naseer Bunda scoring the goal. In 1962, Pakistan won its second Asian Games gold with Chaudhry Ghulam Rasool as captain. At the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Pakistan lost 1–0 to India in the final and finished second in the 1966 Asian Games in Bangkok. Pakistan won its second Olympic gold in 1968 in Mexico City, led by captain Tariq Aziz with key players Saeed Anwar, Khalid Mahmood, Gulraiz Akhtar, and Tariq Niazi. They won all six group matches and defeated West Germany in the knockout round, reaching the final for the fourth consecutive Olympics and winning gold by defeating Australia 2–1, with Muhammad Asad Malik and Abdul Rashid scoring; Rashid scored seven goals, the most, and Tanvir Dar scored six. In the 1970 Asian Games, Pakistan defeated Japan 3–0, Hong Kong 10–0, and drew 0–0 with Thailand, then beat Malaysia 5–0 in the knockout round, and won 1–0 against India in the final to secure its third Asian Games gold. In 1971, the first Hockey World Cup was scheduled in Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War, but due to political tensions between Pakistan and India—especially after a six-year war—and protests led by cricketer Abdul Hafeez Kardar, the FIH moved the tournament to Barcelona, Spain in March 1971. The trophy was formally handed over in Brussels on 27 March 1971 by H.E. Masood, the Pakistani Ambassador to Belgium. Ten teams qualified and were divided into two groups. Pakistan was drawn with Spain, Australia, Japan, and the Netherlands, finishing second in the group behind Spain and advancing to the semi-finals. Pakistan defeated India 2–1 in the first semi-final and lost to Kenya 1–0 in the second semi-final. In the final, Pakistan won 1–0, claiming the first Hockey World Cup, retaining its world number one ranking. Tanvir Dar was the top scorer with eight goals. At the 1972 Munich Olympics, Pakistan lost to West Germany 1–0 and finished fourth. In 1973, they lost to India in the Hockey World Cup. Pakistan won the 1974 Asian Games and retained the title in 1975, but lost to India in the final. In 1976, at the Montreal Olympics, Pakistan won its first bronze medal. In 1978, Pakistan won three major tournaments: the third Hockey World Cup in Buenos Aires, the 1978 Asian Games, and the first Champions Trophy. In 1980, Pakistan boycotted the Moscow Olympics due to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, leading to its absence from the field hockey competition. Pakistan hosted the 1980 and 1981 Champions Trophy, winning the title against West Germany in 1980 and finishing fourth in 1981. In the 1980s, Pakistan won every international tournament it participated in, including the 1982 World Cup in Mumbai and the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles, where they won gold by defeating West Germany. Pakistan also won the Asian Games and Asia Cup consecutively during this period. From the 1970s, hockey was played on synthetic surfaces, and the FIH fully transitioned to AstroTurf in 1986 in London, which made the game faster and shifted focus to strength and pace over stick work and technique. This negatively affected Pakistan, which could not afford to replace grass pitches with expensive synthetic surfaces compared to European nations, leading to a poor performance at the 1986 World Cup, where they won only one pool game and finished 11th. Pakistan gradually recovered and won the 1990 World Cup final as runners-up to the Netherlands and a bronze medal at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona. In 1994, Pakistan won the Champions Trophy at home for the first time in 14 years and later won the Hockey World Cup in Sydney after defeating the Netherlands in a penalty shootout. After the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, Pakistan competed in the 1998 Hockey World Cup in Utrecht, finishing fifth. In 1999, Pakistan won the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup for the first time. At the 2000 Sydney Olympics, Pakistan finished fourth after losing the bronze medal match to Australia, marking the last time the team competed for a medal at the Olympics. In 2002, Pakistan finished fifth at the World Cup and in Kuala Lumpur, winning a bronze medal at the Champions Trophy. At the 2002 Asian Games, Pakistan finished fourth, the first time without a medal. In 2003, Pakistan lost the Hockey Asia Cup final to India. In 2004, Pakistan finished fifth at the Athens Olympics and third at the Champions Trophy in Lahore, securing a third consecutive bronze. In 2005, Pakistan defeated Olympic champion Australia to win the 2005 Hockey RaboTrophy in the Netherlands. In 2006, Pakistan finished sixth at the World Cup and failed to progress from the pool stages of the 2007 Asia Cup. At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Pakistan finished eighth—the worst performance in the team's history. In 2010, Pakistan finished last at the World Cup in New Delhi (12th place) but won the gold medal at the Asian Games in China. In 2011, Pakistan finished seventh at the Olympics and won bronze at the 2012 Champions Trophy in Melbourne after defeating favorites like Germany. The team's most successful tournament during this period was winning the Asian Hockey Champions Trophy in 2012 against India and finishing as runners-up in the inaugural 2011 edition. Despite no major team honors, the team featured world-renowned individual players such as Sohail Abbas, who was top scorer at the 2002 World Cup and 2004 Olympics and later broke the international goals record with 348 goals, and Rehan Butt, twice voted Best Asian Player by the Asian Hockey Federation, along with Shakeel Abbasi, Salman Akbar, and Muhammad Saqlain. Pakistan failed to qualify directly for the 2014 World Cup and was given a last chance by winning the 2013 Asia Cup, but finished third and failed to qualify for the first time in history. Pakistan failed to qualify for the Olympics for the first time at Rio 2016 after failing to qualify in the 2014–15 FIH Hockey World League. From 2016 to 2017, Pakistan performed poorly, including a record 9–1 defeat against Australia in 2017. In 2018, Roelant Oltmans of the Netherlands was appointed coach, and the team showed improvement but still failed to win a match at the 2018 World Cup. Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, losing the qualifiers to the Netherlands in a two-legged tie in 2019. The PHF announced Pakistan's participation in the 2021 Asian Champions Trophy, its first international competition after a two-year gap, with a 20-man squad and Siegfried Aikman as head coach. Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2023 World Cup despite it being a 16-team event. Pakistan participated in the 2022 Commonwealth Games, finishing seventh, and in the 2022 Nations Cup, also finishing seventh. In July 2023, Shahnaz Sheikh was appointed head coach for the 2023 Asian Champions Trophy. In August 2023, the PHF announced a 36-man squad for the Asian Games 2023. In the Asian Games 2023, Pakistan lost 10–2 to India, the biggest defeat in its history, finishing fifth. Pakistan also failed to qualify for the 2024 Summer Olympics. In 2024, Roelant Oltmans was appointed coach for the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup and the Nations Cup. In July 2025, Pakistan's under-18 team lost 3–0 to Japan in the final of the Men's U-18 Asia Cup at the National Hockey Training Centre, highlighting systemic decline due to chronic government neglect, lack of investment in grassroots development, and poor institutional support. Critics argue such defeats reflect broader national apathy toward sports excellence. Pakistan received an invitation from the FIH to compete in the 2025–26 FIH Pro League, qualifying for the tournament. The team's official motif features a star and crescent on a dark green field with a vertical white stripe at the hoist, matching the colors of the Pakistani flag.

Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2024 Summer Olympics. In 2024, Roelant Oltmans was appointed as the coach of Pakistan for the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup and the Nations Cup. In July 2025, Pakistan's under-18 men's team lost 3–0 to Japan in the final of the Men's U-18 Asia Cup, held at the National Hockey Training Centre. Despite showing early aggression and taking multiple penalty corners, Pakistan failed to convert key opportunities, highlighting a systemic decline in the sport due to chronic government neglect, lack of investment in grassroots development, and poor institutional support. Critics argue that such defeats reflect a broader national apathy toward sports excellence. Pakistan received an invitation from the FIH to compete in the 2025–26 FIH Pro League, thereby qualifying for the tournament. The official motif of the Pakistan national field hockey team features a star and crescent on a dark green field, with a vertical white stripe at the hoist, matching the colors of Pakistan's national flag. Pakistan has played at various venues across the country, but by 1978, the primary venue became the National Hockey Stadium in Lahore—also known as Gaddafi Hockey Stadium, named after former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi—considered the largest international field hockey stadium in the world with a capacity of 45,000 spectators. The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) is headquartered at this stadium. Pakistan has hosted numerous international events, including the Hockey Asia Cup in 1982 and the Champions Trophy in 1978, 1980, 1981, 1983, 1984, 1986, 1988, 1992, 1994, 1998, and 2004, as well as the 1990 Hockey World Cup, where Pakistan lost 3–1 to the Netherlands in the final. Since its breakthrough at the 1948 Summer Olympics, Pakistan has won more than 20 official titles.
